1.title: Welcome to Sales at Momence
1.notes: Set the tone. This is not HR orientation — this is sales training. Two weeks from now they should be able to run a real prospecting day end to end. Introduce yourself, the team, and the arc: Day 1 is the job itself, Day 10 is certification.

1.title: How We Work
1.notes: Frame these as how the team operates, not a rules list. Hours/Slack/PTO take 60 seconds. Spend the time on the bottom row: the activity floor is the minimum, not the goal, and HubSpot logging is what makes coaching and commission possible. Meeting-management rules (booking windows, no-shows, cancellations) come on Day 8.

1.title: Your First Two Weeks
1.notes: Walk the arc, don't read the days. Point out the shape: understand the job → understand the buyer → own your list → build the skill → scale it. Emphasize the amber band: pre-vetting is homework that runs the whole two weeks. Reps who keep pre-vetting in downtime go live on Day 10 with a full pool; reps who don't start Day 10 with nothing to call.

1.title: One prospect, four words
1.notes: Do NOT read this as a glossary. Tell it as one story: a pilates studio owner exists → you book her a demo → the AE accepts it against Demo Qualification Criteria, now it's a SAL → the AE moves it to Stage 1 and it's an SQL. Note the handoff: you create the meeting, the AE decides SAL and SQL. Host and TAM are supporting vocabulary only.

1.title: SDRs create qualified pipeline
1.notes: The point of the slide: an SDR is not a call center. If the meetings you create aren't qualified, the engine stalls no matter how many you make. Ask the room: what happens to an AE's month if the SDR fills their calendar with unqualified demos? Everything they do downstream is wasted.

1.title: To book the right meeting, with the right person, at the right time.
1.notes: Have them say the sentence out loud. Then break it: most new SDRs optimize for 'a meeting' and ignore person and time. Right person comes from persona work on Day 2. Right time comes from questions on Day 5 and 6. Right meeting is judged by the Demo Qualification Criteria — that's what turns it into a SAL.

1.title: How an SDR creates revenue
1.notes: Most important visual in the deck. Walk it left to right, then right to left: revenue traces back to one dial. Then point at the ownership bar — you own everything through the booked meeting; the AE decides SAL and SQL. That's not a loophole, it's a quality check on your work.

1.title: The metrics behind the funnel
1.notes: Do not read the numbers — read the right-hand column. The question to keep asking is 'what does this metric buy me?' Calls buy connects, connects buy conversations, conversations buy meetings, meetings buy SALs. If a rep is short on SQLs, we walk backwards up this list to find where the chain broke.

1.title: Leading indicators vs. results
1.notes: This is the mindset slide for a bad week. When results dip, we don't coach the results column — we audit the leading one. Ask: did the activity happen, was the prep real, were the conversations quality, was follow-up done? Fix those and the right column moves on its own.

1.title: 120 Calls Is Not the Job
1.notes: Coaching slide — slow down here. Two reps with identical dial counts can have opposite months. Nobody gets celebrated for 120 calls; they get celebrated for pipeline an AE can close. This is also the argument for taking pre-vetting seriously starting tomorrow.

1.title: Ramp Expectations
1.notes: Month 1 is measured in meetings booked because you don't control AE acceptance yet. From month 2 you're measured on SALs. No basement for the first three ramp months — from 120 days on, the 50% basement applies. Fully Ramped matters for pay: most accelerators require it.

1.title: Compensation
1.notes: Teach the formula, not the table. Variable divided by quota equals what one SAL is worth to you — reps who know their per-SAL number make better decisions about how they spend an hour. Then the two rules: no cliff above 100%, and the 50% basement once you're past 120 days. Don't go deeper than one example; the full plan doc has the rest.

1.title: How you earn more
1.notes: Point out what each one is actually paying for: SQL Rate pays for meeting quality, monthly attainment pays for a big month, Closed Won pays for sourcing real revenue, quarterly pays for consistency. Be explicit that most of these require Fully Ramped — new hires won't be eligible on day one, and that's the incentive to ramp.

1.title: Learn from real calls
1.notes: Set expectations: notes are due Friday and we review them together. The six questions replace 'was this a good call?' — that question teaches nothing. Tell them the goal is pattern recognition before skill: by Day 5 they should already have opinions about what a strong opener sounds like.

1.title: Day 1 Takeaways
1.notes: Close on the three. Don't add anything new. Then tee up Day 2 and make the pre-vetting assignment concrete — they leave today knowing that tomorrow they get leads and start working them in every gap between sessions.

2.title: Who We Sell To + Why
2.notes: Open by connecting to Day 1: yesterday was the job, today is the customer. The four questions on the right are the test — by 5pm they should be able to answer all four about a real business. Flag early that today is when leads land and pre-vetting starts.

2.title: Who we sell to
2.notes: Teach the two types first, then the two tiers. Priority 2 verticals are genuinely Momence customers — momence.com sells to spas, salons and dance schools — but outbound effort goes to Priority 1 while product capabilities catch up. Expect 'so can I book a salon?' — the answer is it's not where your dials go. Trainer note: the June 2025 demo parameters list Salon under do-not-book; that document needs reconciling with this priority model.

2.title: Understand their business before our product
2.notes: Put these up and let the room sit with them. Ask which one they think is hardest to answer from a website. Do NOT let anyone write these down as discovery questions — the next slide shows what each one is really for.

2.title: What each question tells you
2.notes: Pull up a real studio website live and answer four of these in ninety seconds in front of the room. That demonstration is worth more than the slide. What they should leave with: all six are answerable from the outside.

2.title: What problems are we solving?
2.notes: The discipline: a rep who leads with 'we have two-way texting' loses. A rep who leads with 'most studios your size are still chasing no-shows by hand' gets a conversation. Same fact, opposite framing. Read the white half of each card, never the colored half. The next slide gets specific about the three problems you'll actually hear.

2.title: Three problems, over and over
2.notes: These three carry most of your calls. Number two is the one reps underuse — walk the room through booking a class on a competitor site and count the clicks out loud. Number three reframes price: we're not asking them to add a tool, we're asking them to remove three.

2.title: Problem → Impact → Value
2.notes: IMPACT is the step new reps skip, and it's the one that keeps a prospect on the phone. Next slide they run it themselves.

2.title: You have the problem. Find the rest.
2.notes: Split the room into four groups, one problem each, three minutes, then present. Push hard on impact — 'it's annoying' is not an impact. Time, money, or a lost client. Sample answers. 8-step booking: first-time clients abandon and never become customers → two clicks, and we still capture what the business needs. Export/import: data drifts, leads go stale, someone loses a morning → one platform, no handoffs. Manual confirmations: the owner's first hour every day, and no-shows on the days they skip it → automations do it. Four bills: paying four vendors and reconciling between them → one platform, one bill.

2.title: What is our ICP?
2.notes: Say plainly that Momence has no separate ICP document — the qualification parameters define who we sell to, and this is that shape made scannable. Trainer note: Mariana Tek is listed here as do-not-book, but the June 2025 parameters table also lists it among the platforms where 1 bookable staff still qualifies. Those two rules contradict each other and the parameters doc needs updating — until then, do-not-book wins.

2.title: ICP does not mean qualified
2.notes: Tie back to Day 1: SAL is decided by the AE against these parameters. ICP gets a business onto your list; qualification is what makes the meeting count and what makes it pay.

2.title: The right business is only half of it
2.notes: Our source gives one list of qualifying job titles, not a decision-maker/influencer hierarchy — teach it as: these five count, everyone else is a route. Talking to an instructor is fine. Booking a demo with one is not.

2.title: What makes a meeting qualified?
2.notes: Work the right-hand column. Ask why 8 classes and not 3 — below a certain volume there's no scheduling pain to solve. Trainer note: this row still reflects the June 2025 parameters table, which lists Mariana Tek as an accepted platform for the 1-staff exception, while the ICP slide lists it as do-not-book. Flag the contradiction to the room rather than pretending it isn't there.

2.title: Why would someone talk to us?
2.notes: Read it down the page, one line at a time, then ask the room to rebuild it for a business someone names. The teaching point: new reps open at line 5 having never done lines 1 to 4, which is why the line lands flat.

2.title: Building a repeatable framework
2.notes: This replaces the old memorized elevator pitch. Have each rep build parts 2 and 3 out loud for a business they looked at earlier. Then make the fallback concrete: if the site shows nothing, 'most studios on Mindbody tell us booking takes their clients half a dozen steps' is still relevant — it's about their world, not ours.

2.title: Which would you rather hear?
2.notes: Do not advance until the room has argued about it. Have two people read A and B aloud — hearing them matters more than reading them. Take a show of hands and make people defend the choice. The reveal is on the next slide.

2.title: What actually separates them
2.notes: Do the rebuild live on the whiteboard using Riverbend Pilates or whatever business the room named earlier. Show that the rebuilt version is shorter, mentions Momence once, and opens with them. That contrast is the lesson.

2.title: Same Momence. Different conversation.
2.notes: Read down each column first, then across the bottom row. Ask which capability you'd lead with for each and why the other two would be wrong. The bottom row is the only thing that changed.

2.title: So… who should you actually work?
2.notes: Pre-vetting doesn't create more hours, it makes the hours count. The fact-check point matters most on vertical and current-software — those two send reps into bad calls.

2.title: How to pre-vet a lead
2.notes: Stress the order. Business fit first because it's cheapest to check and kills the most records. Persona second. Context last, and only for survivors. Attempting means it's in your working pool with a last-contacted date — no activity for 30 days and it drops to Nurture, so don't park records there and forget them.

2.title: Minimum viable research
2.notes: Name the trap: research feels like work, so an anxious rep spends forty minutes on one account and calls it a productive morning. The three questions are the stopping rule.

2.title: Live practice
2.notes: Intended answers, one at a time. 1) BUSINESS FIT: yes — class based, pilates is Priority 1, physical location, working website, 11 weekly in-person classes clears the 8+ bar. 2) PERSONA FIT: yes — Studio Manager and Founder are both qualifying titles; the 3 instructors are staff, a route not a booking. 3) CONTEXT: they're on Mindbody — a competitor platform, not a disqualifier, and it means booking pain is already proven. Good opener material: their clients are going through a multi-step booking flow today. 4) DECISION: Attempting — into the working pool. Push the room on why Mindbody isn't a reason to skip it.

2.title: Pre-vet now, and never stop
2.notes: Make the stakes concrete: on Day 10 two reps go live, one with a vetted pool and one without, and by lunch they're having completely different days. Then land the last line hard — this never stops. A rep who quits pre-vetting in month three has a dead pipeline in month four, and they will not see it coming until the SALs stop.

2.title: Day 2 Takeaways
2.notes: Close on the three, then send them to their leads. Everyone leaves knowing where their list is and that the expectation starts today, not Day 4.

3.title: Owning Your Book of Business
3.notes: Day 1 was the job, Day 2 was the customer, today is the thing you actually own. Set the frame immediately: nobody is going to hand you a list every Monday any more. What's in front of you is yours to manage, and how well you manage it is what your month looks like.

3.title: What is a Book of Business?
3.notes: Land the last line hard. New reps assume more leads equals more meetings. It doesn't — a rep with 800 well-managed accounts will beat a rep with 2,000 they've never sorted. Everything today follows from that.

3.title: This one is yours to run
3.notes: Frame this as an upgrade, not a warning. Most SDR jobs hand you a list and you call it — here you get to decide, which is more interesting work and it compounds: the better you know your Book, the better every day gets. The loop at the bottom is the whole of Day 3, and the next slides are one lap around it.

3.title: Understand before you act
3.notes: Question 3 is the one reps skip. Somebody may have had a real conversation with this account six months ago — calling it cold and repeating a pitch they already rejected is how you burn an account. The status is the shortcut, but the activity history is the detail.

3.title: The four statuses you actively work
3.notes: Read the colored blocks across, left to right — that is the whole slide. The 30-day rule on Attempting is the one to hammer: a rep who lets accounts go quiet is silently shrinking their own working pool every month, and they won't notice until their dial list is empty.

3.title: Where every lead ends up
3.notes: Trace one account all the way around: new lead, you dial, no answer, it goes Attempting. You keep at it, they say not interested, it drops to Nurture. Three months later it's Recycled and back in your working pool. Nothing disappears — it circulates. That's why dispositioning honestly matters: the automation is only as good as what you log.

3.title: Why we code
3.notes: Ask the room: you had a great call on Tuesday with an owner who said call me in March. It's now March and you have 1,400 accounts. How do you find her? That's the whole argument for coding — memory doesn't scale and notes you can't filter are invisible.

3.title: Choosing the right code
3.notes: Work these live — read the situation, take a vote, then reveal. The distinction reps blur is AF1 vs AF2: both are pre-vetted and bookable. AF1 hits every single box; AF2 is slightly off on one, like enough classes but short on staff. The vertical doesn't decide it — a drop-in dance studio set up like a yoga or Pilates studio that hits every box is AF1. Keep that honest or your AF1 list stops meaning anything. AFH is the one code that isn't about fit — it's about timing, and it earns the top of your list. AFU marks an account that doesn't fit today, because it misses parameters or runs on software we can't target right now, like ClubReady. Coding it keeps you from re-working it next month and lets you find it again if that changes. Note that AF1 and AF2 are what connect Day 2's pre-vetting assignment to this Book — a pre-vetted account nobody coded is an account you can't find again.

3.title: Not every lead deserves attention today
3.notes: The amber band is the most common failure mode on this team. A rep finds one list that works, runs it into the ground, and never touches New or Recycled — so the Book quietly rots while their activity numbers look fine.

3.title: Who do I work first?
3.notes: Be explicit that this is the answer to 'what do I do when I sit down.' There is no priority score in our process — the order is the process. Step 06 is the honest one: whichever half you skipped in step 02, you owe it before the day ends.

3.title: Needs attention now vs. worked later
3.notes: New reps take a no personally and either argue with it or quietly stop dispositioning honestly. Both are worse than the no. Show them that the process turns a no into a scheduled second shot — but only if they log it.

3.title: Why we segment
3.notes: The distinction that costs reps time: they build a static list on Monday, work it all week, and half of it has changed status by Wednesday. Standing views should be active. A finite batch you intend to finish can be static.

3.title: From Book of Business to a list you can finish
3.notes: The funnel is the point: a Book is not workable, a list is. Show that the same Book produces four completely different lists depending on the job you picked. Job 03 is the housekeeping one nobody does — clearing Unqualified accounts out is what keeps the other three lists honest.

3.title: Maintain Your Book
3.notes: The 25-a-day number is the maintenance habit that makes everything else possible. Frame it as replacement, not extra work: four leads left your Book today, so four have to come back in. A rep who skips this for a month has a Book that can't produce a call list.

3.title: What would you work first?
3.notes: Take answers before revealing. Intended order: D first — it is at 27 days and drops to Nurture at 30, so if nobody touches it today you lose it out of the working pool for three months. Then A — AFH, a named callback this week from someone in market, the closest thing to a live opportunity in the set. Then B — AF1, pre-vetted and a strong fit, zero research left, a pure dial. Then E — AF2, back in play, but it needs an opener that acknowledges the renewal objection, so it takes a few minutes of preparation first. C is the trap: do nothing. It is mid-cooling-period, and calling it now wastes both the lead and the dial. The lesson worth landing: the most urgent account was the one with no code and no recent activity, and most rooms pick A because it feels the best.

3.title: Day 3 Takeaways
3.notes: Close on the three lines, then make tomorrow concrete: they should arrive with the accounts they couldn't decide on. Day 4 is only useful if they've actually been doing the work since Day 2.

4.title: Pre-Vetting Workshop
4.notes: FACILITATOR PREP — before delivering Day 4, pull real pre-vetting examples and edge cases from the reps' actual work since Day 2. This deck is deliberately thin on scenarios because the material is supposed to come from them. Open by saying plainly: today is not new information, it's reps getting better at something they've already been doing for two days.

4.title: The framework you've been using
4.notes: Sixty seconds on this slide. The top row is the Day 2 framework, the bottom row is the same thing as a working sequence. Pause on step 5 — it is the last thing you do before an account leaves your pre-vetting queue, and it has two parts: the code, and the information. The code is how you find the account again in a list. The information is what you actually say when you get them on the phone. A note with one and not the other is half a job.

4.title: What have you run into so far?
4.notes: Do not rush this. Ten minutes minimum, and write the answers somewhere visible — you'll reference them on slides 6 and 8. If the room is quiet, go first with a real example of your own. The single most useful question is the third one: reps rarely notice which step is eating their time until they're asked out loud.

4.title: What good pre-vetting looks like
4.notes: Four questions, and every one of them ends in a decision you have to make anyway. If a piece of research doesn't help answer one of the four, it isn't pre-vetting — it's procrastinating. The note is the part reps skip: research you didn't write down is research you're going to do again.

4.title: Accuracy vs. speed
4.notes: Reps hear 'be faster' and assume we want them cutting corners — say the opposite out loud. We have no time limit on pre-vetting and we're not introducing one. The speed comes from knowing what you're looking for, not from skipping steps. Ask the room which of the two outer columns they think is their own failure mode; most will say too much.

4.title: Where this usually gets sticky
4.notes: Tie each row back to what the room said on slide 3 — if nobody raised it, don't dwell on it. Source note: our Pre-Vetting 101 material doesn't carry an explicit list of common mistakes, so these five are drawn from its own warnings and best practices. Replace any of them with the real friction the reps named.

4.title: Research that actually matters
4.notes: This one question is the whole slide, and it's the fastest way to cut research time without losing accuracy. Run it live against something a rep researched this week — a studio's Instagram following, say. Does it change whether you call them, who you call, or your opener? If not, that's a tab you didn't need to open.

4.title: Pull up your own leads
4.notes: FACILITATOR — this is the bulk of the session. Have your own set of real examples pulled in advance in case the room brings thin ones, and screen-share each account as you work it. Make reps say their decision out loud before you give yours, and connect every one back to the four questions on slide 4. Item 5 is the one to hunt for: an account someone spent twenty minutes on and still left undecided is the single most instructive example you can get.

4.title: Good pre-vetting is…
4.notes: Keep this short. Read the three words, read the two lines on the band, and stop. The last line is the permission reps actually need — most of them are over-researching because nobody has told them when they're allowed to stop.

4.title: Keep building your callable pool
4.notes: Land the Day 10 point — it's the reason any of this matters to them personally. Then send them back to their Book. If the session ran long, this is the slide to read fast; the previous one carries the lesson.

5.title: Cold Calling Fundamentals
5.notes: FACILITATOR PREP — pull 2-3 real Momence cold calls before delivering Day 5, ideally with different strengths and coaching opportunities. They're used in the Call Breakdown on slide 14. Open by reading the panel on the right out loud. Everything today hangs off it: a rep who tries to sell the product on a cold call loses; a rep who creates enough relevance to earn fifteen minutes wins.

5.title: What a cold call is actually for
5.notes: Ask the room what they think the goal of a cold call is — most will say 'book a meeting', which is right but incomplete. The meeting is the outcome; relevance is the mechanism. A rep who opens by explaining the product has skipped straight to the thing the AE is paid to do.

5.title: The anatomy of a great cold call
5.notes: Show the mapping explicitly so nobody thinks we changed the process. Our cold call training has four steps; this breaks the first one into three, because 'Intro' is where almost every call is won or lost and 'make it your own' isn't enough instruction on its own. Closing the meeting — confirming time, calendar, next step — is Day 8 and deliberately greyed out here.

5.title: The first ten seconds
5.notes: Resist giving them one opener — they will memorize it and it will sound memorized. The judgment call is which type fits the human who answered, and they'll know within about two words. Have the room say the example line out loud in their own words, three different ways.

5.title: Getting past the gatekeeper
5.notes: The mistake reps make is treating the gatekeeper as an obstacle to beat rather than a person to work with. Pitching them wastes the only shot you get — they can't buy, and now they know what you want. The amber callout is worth a real example: if the person asking 'what's this regarding' knows their class schedule and their software, you're already talking to the decision maker.

5.title: Where your pre-vetting shows up
5.notes: This is the payoff slide for Days 2 through 4. The middle column is the one reps skip — knowing the facts isn't the same as knowing what those facts mean for a business like this. Have them build all three columns live for an account in their own Book.

5.title: Discovery, not interrogation
5.notes: Note that the first question is deliberately positive — asking what they love gets people talking, and the second question is where the pain comes out. Reps who lead with 'what's frustrating about your software' get a defensive answer. Don't let anyone write these down as a required sequence; they're openers for a conversation.

5.title: Listen for the thread
5.notes: Our pitch training says the best way to pivot is to ask a question — this is that, applied to listening. When a prospect volunteers a problem, that is the most valuable sentence in the call, and a rep who moves past it to their own agenda has thrown it away. Play a recording and stop it the moment a thread appears; ask the room what they'd say next.

5.title: Connect the problem to value
5.notes: The bottom row is what our own training says these owners care about — not a feature list. A rep who hears 'no-shows' and responds with retention is relevant; a rep who responds with the full platform is noise. Say plainly: name one thing, then move. You are not the demo.

5.title: Pitch in the conversation, not at them
5.notes: Read the left-hand quote out loud in a flat voice — the room will hear exactly why it fails, and every one of those capabilities is true. Being true isn't the problem; being unprompted is. Then read the right-hand version. Half the words, one capability, and it ends with a question.

5.title: When you've earned the ask
5.notes: The most common way reps lose a booked meeting is by continuing to sell after the prospect was already willing. Ask the room how they'll know — the honest answer is that they'll feel it, and the discipline is going for it rather than adding one more proof point.

5.title: Direct. Confident. Simple.
5.notes: Have every rep say the good version out loud with a real day and time. Most will soften it on the first try — 'would maybe Thursday possibly work' — and hearing themselves do it is the lesson. Do not go into confirmation or calendar mechanics; that's Day 8 and it will swallow the session.

5.title: The full call flow
5.notes: If a rep only remembers one thing from today, make it the ability to answer 'where am I in this call right now?' That question is what stops a rep from pitching during discovery or asking for a meeting before they've earned it.

5.title: Call breakdown
5.notes: FACILITATOR — you need 2-3 real Momence cold calls queued before this session, ideally showing different strengths so reps see more than one way it can go well. Stop the recording at each stage rather than playing it through; ask the room to name the stage before you name it. A call with a coaching opportunity is more useful than a perfect one.

5.title: Role play
5.notes: Pair reps and rotate who plays the prospect. Give the prospect a real account from their own Book so the details are true. Resist letting rounds run long — the value is in repetition, not in one perfect run. If someone gets stuck on an objection, note it for tomorrow and move on rather than coaching it now.

5.title: Three things to leave with
5.notes: Read the three, read the band, stop. Then send them to dial. The best thing that can happen after Day 5 is a rep having a bad call and knowing exactly which stage it fell apart in.

5.title: Controlling the Conversation
5.notes: Name the four words and move on — do not start teaching the framework, and do not take objection questions beyond 'we cover that tomorrow.' If role play surfaced good objections today, write them down and open Day 6 with them.

6.title: Controlling the Conversation
6.notes: FACILITATOR PREP — before Day 6, pull real/common Momence objections, real call clips where objections appear, and examples of both strong and coachable handling. Those drive the Objection Lab and role play. Open by naming the reframe: yesterday assumed the call went well. Today is every call that doesn't, which is most of them.

6.title: Why prospects push back
6.notes: Tell the Home Depot story properly — ask the room how many of them have said 'just looking' and then wandered around unable to find the thing. That reflex is exactly what a rep hears in the first eight seconds of a cold call, and reps take it personally because they think it's a verdict. It isn't. It's a script, and the whole framework exists to break it.

6.title: Not every “no” is the same
6.notes: Our source material lists these objections but doesn't label them objection vs brush-off — that sort is a teaching device, and the footnote says so. The practical point: reps respond to 'just send me info' with a product answer, when what it actually needs is a better reason to be on the phone at all.

6.title: The biggest mistake is answering too fast
6.notes: 'Give your brain time to react' is straight from our own objection material and it's the most underrated line in it. Acknowledging buys you two seconds of thinking time while sounding like empathy rather than a stall. Demonstrate it: have someone throw you an objection and answer instantly, then answer again after acknowledging. The room hears the difference immediately.

6.title: Acknowledge → Disarm → Add Value → Ask
6.notes: Our own material says: walk through these but don't explain them yet — ask the room what they think each one means and why it exists, then let the next four slides confirm it. That collaboration is more effective than defining them at people. The bottom row is the stated purpose of the whole discipline.

6.title: Show them you actually heard it
6.notes: Ask the question on the dark bar and let the room answer before you reveal it. The failure mode our material calls out: a rep hears the prospect, says 'ok, whatever, let's take a call' — and that turns into a no, a not-interested, or a hang-up. Acknowledging isn't politeness, it's the thing that makes the next three steps land.

6.title: Break the buyer script
6.notes: This is where the Home Depot analogy pays off — disarming is the employee saying 'no problem, I'll be over there if you need me,' which is the only response that ever makes you come back. Note for the trainer: these are the two disarm examples in our objection material. If the team uses others — 'this is just an introduction', 'we aren't even sure we'd be the right fit' — add them, but they aren't in the deck we have.

6.title: Give them a reason to keep going
6.notes: Lean into their pain — that's the instruction from our pitch material and it's the difference between value and noise. Note there are no numbers on this slide on purpose: our source material makes no quantitative claims about hours saved or revenue gained, so reps shouldn't either. If someone wants a stat, tell them to bring it to the AE conversation.

6.title: Give the conversation somewhere to go
6.notes: This is the step reps drop under pressure — they acknowledge, disarm, add value, then stop talking and wait to be rescued. The prospect fills that silence with 'anyway, send me something.' Make the room practice ending every single response with a question, even a small one.

6.title: How it sounds as one conversation
6.notes: Read all four lines aloud as one continuous response, then read them again with a beat between each so the room hears how robotic the stitched version sounds. The Add Value line is deliberately not a stat — it's one relevant capability tied to what they just said.

6.title: The framework holds. The words don't.
6.notes: Point out which parts stayed the same: acknowledge and disarm are nearly identical across both columns because they respond to the emotion, not the facts. Value and ask are where the pre-vetting and the listening show up. A rep who memorized one response gets the second call wrong.

6.title: Redirect, don't debate
6.notes: Every rep knows not to say the red line, and under pressure a surprising number say a softer version of it. Watch for 'actually, a lot of studios find…' — that's the same move wearing a nicer jacket. You cannot argue someone into a meeting.

6.title: Know when to keep going
6.notes: There is no 'three objections and stop' rule in our material and we're not inventing one. What we do have is the disposition process from Day 3, and that's the real answer: the system is built so an honest no comes back to you in three months. Reps who push past a clear no are trading a future Recycled lead for a Dead one.

6.title: Build the response, out loud
6.notes: FACILITATOR — these six come from our own cold call training. Swap in whatever the team is actually hearing this month. Run it live: throw the objection, pick a rep, make them build all four steps out loud before anyone else speaks. The four questions at the bottom are the coaching, not the response itself.

6.title: Partner role play
6.notes: Coach hard against scripted delivery — the moment a rep sounds like they're reciting, stop them and make them say it conversationally. Rotate who plays the prospect and tell the prospect to be realistic, not cruel. A prospect who hangs up instantly teaches nothing.

6.title: Four things, in order
6.notes: Read the four words, read the framework, read the band. Then stop. The last line is the whole day in one sentence.

6.title: Working Smarter at Scale
6.notes: Name the six words and stop. If the role play surfaced objections nobody could handle, note them and bring them back — but don't start teaching Day 7 material now.

7.title: Working Smarter at Scale
7.notes: FACILITATOR PREP — reps must have their REAL Book of Business open and accessible for slide 13. Do not run that exercise on a manufactured example; the whole point is that they leave with a plan for tomorrow's actual leads. Open by naming the shift: Days 1–6 taught them how to work one prospect. Today is about hundreds of them, and the difference between a rep who books consistently and one who doesn't is almost never how hard they worked.

7.title: Activity isn't strategy
7.notes: Be careful with the framing here — this is not permission to do less. Reps still owe their daily activity. The point is that two reps making the same number of dials can produce completely different results, and the difference is decided before the first dial. Ask the room: has anyone opened the dialer and just started calling whatever appeared? Most hands go up. That's the behavior we're replacing.

7.title: The loop you run every day
7.notes: Say plainly that this is not a new framework — it's the Day 3 funnel with three more steps on the end. If a rep thinks they now have two competing systems, we've failed. Keep this slide visible in the room; the first half of the day is one pass around this loop.

7.title: Who deserves my attention today?
7.notes: Deliberately short — Day 3 taught prioritization in full and this is a reinforcement, not a re-teach. There is no scoring system at Momence; the signals on this slide are the ones reps already own. The line that matters is the indigo band: a dialer will happily serve up whatever list is loaded, and a rep who lets it choose has outsourced the most important decision of their day.

7.title: A list needs a reason to exist
7.notes: The three standard filters at the bottom are the ones our own Lists 101 material requires on every list — they are the floor, not the strategy. Everything strategic is what you add after them. Emphasize the third test: a list of 4,000 contacts isn't a segment, it's your Book with a filter on it. Orum's own guidance is a maximum of 1,000 contacts in a dialing list, and past that you have to refresh mid-session.

7.title: Different leads need different plays
7.notes: These four come from our own list-building material and from the statuses and codes on Day 3 — vertical, current software, last activity, status and code are all named filters in Lists 101. Do not add categories to fill space. Ask the room for a fifth and pressure-test it against the middle column: if they can't say why the group is together in one sentence, it doesn't survive.

7.title: Let the reason pick the action
7.notes: The parallel-vs-power rule is straight from our own Orum best practices and it's the most concrete decision on this slide: a warm lead burned in a parallel dial is a lead you don't get back. Don't go deep on sequence strategy — flag it and move. GAP: our source material doesn't define which segments are supposed to go into a sequence versus a call list. If that rule exists on this team, get it from the manager and add it; we are not inventing one.

7.title: Orum executes the strategy. It doesn't create it.
7.notes: Say clearly that we are not teaching Orum mechanics here — the prerecorded videos cover session setup, list selection and the metrics screens. What matters live is the sequencing: leads, segment, context, then dial. The 'SDR Additional Notes' field is the same one they filled in during pre-vetting on Day 4, and this is where that work pays off, because it's what they see mid-call.

7.title: One attempt isn't a strategy
7.notes: Keep this conceptual — Day 9 is Multichannel Prospecting and it owns the detail. The one concrete thing to land is dispositioning, because it's the mechanism behind everything: Orum only completes a sequence call task on a connect, no answer or voicemail, and our own status automation moves a lead based on what gets logged. GAP: we have no documented Momence cadence — number of touches, spacing, channel order. If one exists, it belongs on Day 9, not invented here.

7.title: Your funnel tells you what's broken
7.notes: Say the caveat out loud: connect rate is our own number — 5% is what we average, and that's the one to hold yourself to. The conversation, meeting, bridged and callback figures are Orum's published benchmarks from their own data, not Momence targets. The point of the slide isn't the numbers — it's that the chain only runs one direction. You can't fix meetings by working on your ask if you aren't getting connects. Also worth naming: a callback is 4x more likely to book than a cold dial, which is why the callback number is on this slide at all.

7.title: Diagnose the conversion point first
7.notes: Guard the framing hard: none of these are diagnoses. A low connect rate can be data, timing, number type or provider quality, and a rep who assumes it's one of those without checking will fix the wrong thing. Everything in column two and three is a skill we already taught — Day 5 for the opener and discovery, Day 6 for resistance. This slide is where the week starts pointing back at itself.

7.title: Adjust before you add
7.notes: Three starting points, not three rules. The habit we want is a rep who looks at their own funnel before their 1:1 and arrives with a hypothesis instead of waiting to be told. Reinforce that more activity is a legitimate answer when the top of the funnel is genuinely thin — the failure is reaching for it automatically, every time, regardless of what the numbers say.

7.title: Build tomorrow's plan
7.notes: FACILITATOR PREP — reps need their actual Book of Business open for this. Do not substitute a sample set; a manufactured exercise teaches the shape of the answer and none of the judgment. Walk the room while they build. The most common failure is question 03: a rep will have a segment that is really just 'my leads with a filter on it', and the reason won't survive being said out loud. That's the whole lesson, so let it happen rather than preventing it.

7.title: Five words, in order
7.notes: Keep it short. If a rep leaves with one thing, it's that the loop closes — reassess feeds tomorrow's priority, which is why this is a system rather than five separate habits.

7.title: From “Yes” to Meeting Held
7.notes: Close on the shift in responsibility: up to now a booked meeting has felt like the finish line, and tomorrow we treat it as the start of a handoff they own. Don't preview the content beyond the five words.

8.title: From “Yes” to Meeting Held
8.notes: FACILITATOR PREP — before Day 8, pull: one REAL strong AE handoff and one REAL weak one (slide 7), and two or three real meeting-protection situations from the team — an unaccepted invite, a cancellation, a no-show, and a meeting booked too far out. Those get discussed live; there is no scenario slide. Open by asking how many reps think their job is done when the meeting goes on the calendar, then spend the day dismantling it.

8.title: A booking isn't pipeline
8.notes: Tie the first card back to the demo qualification parameters from Day 2 — we are not adding criteria here, just reminding them the bar hasn't moved because someone said yes. The middle card is the whole day. Note that our own booking material says preventing a no-show starts while you're still on the call, which is why we're spending the next three slides there.

8.title: Finish the call strong
8.notes: The checklist is ours, verbatim from the booking material — the four-step framework above it is just the reasoning underneath it. Don't teach the scheduling link here; that's a prerecorded video. What to land: reps rush this because they're relieved, and the rushed version is the one that no-shows.

8.title: Book it close
8.notes: Be honest about the evidence: our booking deck says show rate in 0–3 days is significantly higher and gives no figure, so don't let anyone leave thinking there's a published percentage. If a prospect genuinely can't meet inside three days, book what they'll take — but flag it to yourself as a meeting that will need more protection, and say so on slide 12.

8.title: Make it real while you still have them
8.notes: Those three lines are the actual talk tracks from our booking material — teach them as patterns, not a script, exactly like Day 5. The third one is the most underused: naming a deadline for the acceptance gives you a legitimate, non-pushy reason to call back. GAP: our material doesn't say who attends besides the AE and the prospect, so 'who's attending' means naming the AE and asking whether anyone else on their side should be there.

8.title: The AE should not walk in blind
8.notes: Our own material is blunt about this: be as specific and granular as possible, no such thing as TMI. Pinning matters because an unpinned note is a note nobody finds. The intro email is part of the handoff, not a courtesy — it introduces the AE by name to the prospect and puts the AE on the thread. Mechanics of both are prerecorded.

8.title: What makes it strong
8.notes: FACILITATOR — replace the strong example with a real one from your team before you deliver, and bring a real weak one too. The illustration here is written to match our required fields (business type, locations, classes, current software, job title) plus the reason for the meeting; it is an example of the shape, not a real account. GAP: our material lists the required fields and says the notes should be granular, but doesn't define a required structure for the notes themselves — this four-part frame is a teaching device.

8.title: Your job doesn't end at the calendar event
8.notes: Both quoted lines are ours — 'hold your prospect's hand' and 'the responsibility is yours, not the AE's' come straight from the show-rate material. The second one is the one reps resist, so name it directly: an AE who gets no-showed lost an hour, but the SDR lost the credit and the pipeline.

8.title: The calendar invite tells you something
8.notes: Those three are our actual follow-up talk tracks. The framing to hold: an unaccepted invite is information, not an insult. Push back on any rep who treats a chase as begging — you told them on the call you'd check, so calling is keeping your word. GAP: our material covers the day before and the morning of, but says nothing about the window between booking and the day before. If a meeting is booked five days out, use your judgment and flag it.

8.title: Follow-up should reduce friction
8.notes: This is our documented cadence, said plainly and without the swagger the old deck had. Two things to police in the room: the attempt counts are a ceiling for a meeting that isn't confirmed, not a quota to hit on every booking; and 'assumptive' means you don't pre-emptively offer a reschedule, it does not mean you ignore someone telling you they can't make it. GAP: the cadence assumes at least a day of lead time. For a same-day or next-morning booking, our material doesn't say — use judgment.

8.title: Match the response to what actually happened
8.notes: Every element here is ours: the five-minute AE notification, the No Show Sequence, the leave-me-alone versus timing distinction, and 'a no is better than a ghost.' On a leave-me-alone cancel, the honest question is whether the booking call was actually a yes — that's a coaching moment about slide 5, not just a lost meeting. Our material also suggests looping in a teammate or manager on a stalled reschedule; a different voice sometimes lands where yours won't.

8.title: Low show rate: where should I look?
8.notes: Same discipline as Day 7 slide 11 — these are places to investigate, not causes. Have reps pick the column they're weakest on and say it out loud. The fifth one is the uncomfortable one: a soft yes taken to hit a number shows up two weeks later as a no-show, and the fix is on the cold call, not in the follow-up. GAP: our material publishes no show-rate target and no benchmark, so there is no number on this slide. If the team sets one, add it.

8.title: Four things, in order
8.notes: Short close. If one line survives the day, it's that the responsibility is theirs and not the AE's — everything else on the deck follows from accepting that.

8.title: Multichannel Prospecting
8.notes: Close by pointing at today: they've already used three channels to protect a meeting — call, email, text. Tomorrow is about doing that deliberately at the front of the funnel instead of only after a booking. Don't preview past the four words.

9.title: Multichannel Prospecting
9.notes: FACILITATOR PREP — before Day 9, pull three or four REAL Momence SDR emails worth discussing (strong ones, and one that was busy without being relevant); prepare the prospect context you'll hand the room for the workshop on slide 12; and confirm reps have their real Book of Business accessible for slide 13. Open by naming the trap: reps who discover email usually use it to stop calling. That is the opposite of the lesson.

9.title: More channels, not more noise
9.notes: The callback to Day 8 is the fastest way to land this — they already ran a three-channel play, they just ran it after a booking. Today moves it to the front of the funnel. Push on the left column: a rep who sends the same message three ways isn't being persistent, they're being ignored three times.

9.title: The call is still the center
9.notes: Say the bottom line out loud and mean it. Email feels productive and safe, and it's the most common place a new rep hides. Watch dial counts for the two weeks after this session — if they dip, this slide didn't land.

9.title: Context → Intent → Channel → Message
9.notes: This is the spine of the day and every remaining slide hangs off it. Make them practice the intent sentence out loud — 'I want to restart a conversation that stalled two weeks ago after she said they'd just renewed' is an intent. 'Follow up' is not.

9.title: Each channel has a job
9.notes: GAP — flag this plainly. We have no documented SMS methodology beyond two specific uses: offering a text instead of an email when a prospect wants links, and the meeting-protection texts from Day 8. Everything else on the SMS card is those two uses restated. Do not extend it into cold SMS outreach; if this team wants an SMS play, it needs to be written and approved first.

9.title: Write it the way they read it
9.notes: All four rows are from our own email material. Two honesty notes for the room. First: our material claims short subject lines lift open rates but publishes no evidence, so teach the rule and skip the claim. Second — GAP — our material raises an interest-based CTA and then explicitly disagrees with it, which means we have no settled position on the ask. Say so, and teach the CTA the way Day 5 teaches the meeting ask: direct, specific, easy to answer. Our material also mentions the trick of pulling three random words from the body for the subject line; it's hedged in the source and it isn't a Momence standard.

9.title: Personalization isn't relevance
9.notes: Both examples are illustrations of the pattern, not real Momence emails — say so. They're built on things reps actually find in pre-vetting (schedule, class count) and on the admin-burden problem from Day 2, and neither makes a product claim. Ask the room what the first email's ask even is; there isn't one, which is why it gets no reply.

9.title: Write from the problem, not the product
9.notes: The product-first example uses our own approved positioning line — which is the point: it's accurate and it still doesn't work in a cold email. The prospect-first version draws on the manual-admin problem from Day 2 and makes no capability claim at all. Reps will want to add a second problem; don't let them. The email's job is one reply, not a full pitch.

9.title: Every interaction creates context for the next one
9.notes: The “Just called” subject line is ours — our email material says follow-ups should go warm, and names that exact phrasing. Walk this example live rather than reading it. The tell for a rep who isn't doing this: their email would be identical whether the call went to voicemail or the owner talked to them for four minutes.

9.title: The outcome decides the follow-up
9.notes: Note what this slide deliberately isn't: a cadence. We have no documented Momence touch pattern — no number of attempts, no spacing, no channel order — so we're not inventing one. The middle column is the part to hold reps to; the right column is a suggestion. 'Send me information' should trigger the Day 6 reflex: that's a brush-off, and the email that follows it needs to earn attention, not just attach something.

9.title: Your outreach should feel connected
9.notes: The five-touch example is an illustration of context-driven decisions, not a prescribed pattern — say that before you walk it. Connect the bottom line back to Day 7: a sequence is an execution tool for a segment you already decided on, and it doesn't relieve anyone of thinking. GAP: we have no documented Momence cadence, so if the team runs standard sequences, the facilitator should show them here rather than have reps assume one exists.

9.title: One prospect. One email. Ten minutes.
9.notes: FACILITATOR — bring real prospect context for this: a business type, size, current software, and something that came out of a call. Don't hand out a fictional case study. Read two or three aloud without naming the author and ask the room which one they'd reply to and why. Also bring the real Momence SDR emails you pulled and read one of those last, so the room sees what good looks like in practice.

9.title: Now do it with your own prospects
9.notes: FACILITATOR PREP — reps need their real Book open for this. Walk the room; the failure mode is question 02, where 'follow up' gets offered as an intent. Push until they name what they actually want to happen. Tie the logging note back to Day 3 and Day 8: the next touch can only build on the last one if the last one was written down.

9.title: Three things, in order
9.notes: Short close. The line at the bottom is the one to leave them with — it's the same test as slide 4's intent sentence, just phrased as a filter.

9.title: Put It All Together
9.notes: Don't teach any of the workflow tonight — the panel is a map, not a lesson. The message is that nothing new is coming, which is either reassuring or terrifying depending on the rep, and both are useful.

10.title: Put It All Together
10.notes: FACILITATOR PREP — seven things must be finalized before you deliver Day 10, and none of them exist in the onboarding materials: (1) the certification scorecard and rubric, (2) the passing criteria, (3) the cold-call role-play scenarios for slide 7, (4) which objections you'll introduce during certification, (5) the process for a rep who doesn't pass on the first attempt, (6) confirmation that every rep has access to their real Book of Business, and (7) confirmation that the prerecorded reference library is organized and reachable. Set expectations at the top: roughly a quarter of today is slides, the rest is them working. Nothing new gets taught.

10.title: The SDR system
10.notes: Spend real time here — this is the first time they see the whole thing as one connected system rather than ten separate days. Walk it once, left to right, naming the day each stage came from. Then point at the loop symbol: analyze and adjust feed straight back into tomorrow's priority, which is the Day 7 lesson and the reason this is a system rather than a checklist.

10.title: The workflow is a series of decisions
10.notes: This slide sets the tone for the whole day. Tell them plainly that 'why' is coming after every answer, and that a rep who can defend a debatable decision beats a rep who lands the textbook answer and can't say how they got there. That is the actual bar.

10.title: From lead to meeting held
10.notes: Keep this fast — it's a recap, not a lesson. Ask the room which row they feel least confident about and note it; that's where you push hardest during their certification.

10.title: Your Book of Business
10.notes: Ask 'why' relentlessly here — a rep who prioritizes correctly by instinct but can't explain the reasoning will not repeat it under pressure next week. Watch for the Day 3 failure mode: a rep who only ever works Attempting because those accounts have history, and never touches New or Recycled.

10.title: Prospect strategy
10.notes: Five prospects, not one — the point is to see whether the reasoning holds up across a range rather than on their single best account. Have them present two or three live; all five get written up and sent to their manager by end of day, which is also the first thing that manager has in writing about how this rep thinks. A rep who says a prospect isn't worth pursuing and explains it well has passed this exercise — arguably better than one who forces a bad fit into a yes. Push on the last two boxes especially: 'I'd tell them about Momence' is not a problem to lead with.

10.title: The cold call
10.notes: FACILITATOR — bring your own role-play scenarios and decide in advance which objections you'll introduce; neither is built into this deck on purpose. Run the objections in the order that fits the conversation, not a fixed script. If a rep freezes, let it sit for a beat before rescuing them — Day 6 taught that the pause is the point.

10.title: How you're evaluated
10.notes: FACILITATOR — the scorecard, the weighting, the passing threshold and the retry process are all yours to define and none of them are in this deck. Walk the room through your rubric here, verbally, before certification starts, so nobody is guessing at the bar they're being held to.

10.title: Coach yourself
10.notes: Push them to come to their first 1:1 with a hypothesis rather than waiting to be told what's wrong. That habit is the difference between a rep who improves in month two and one who plateaus.

10.title: Your first week live
10.notes: Say the activity numbers out loud from the Day 1 deck rather than paraphrasing them, so there's no ambiguity about what starts tomorrow. Then land the last card: nothing on this slide is a new rule, which is the point — the routine they practiced for nine days is the routine, full stop.

10.title: Your reference library
10.notes: FACILITATOR — confirm the library is actually organized and reachable before you show this slide; pointing reps at a folder that doesn't exist undoes the credibility of the whole day. Say plainly that asking where a video is costs nothing, and guessing at a workflow costs a lead.

10.title: You need to know how to make the next right decision.
10.notes: Close the ten days here. Don't add a summary — the room has had enough content. If certifications ran long, this slide is the one thing worth stopping for.
